reference.source: Kelley & Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology / large-vessel vasculitis guidance
clinicalPearls: Often discovered incidentally when aortic tissue removed at aneurysm surgery shows inflammation without a preceding systemic diagnosis
Histology commonly demonstrates giant-cell or lymphoplasmacytic inflammation of the aortic wall
By definition there are no features of a defined systemic vasculitis or infection at presentation
The thoracic aorta, particularly the ascending segment, is the most frequent site
Aneurysm formation and dissection are the principal structural risks
A proportion of patients later declare a systemic large-vessel vasculitis such as giant-cell arteritis, warranting follow-up
Postoperative imaging surveillance is needed because disease may progress at other aortic segments
reference.pathophysiology: Clinically isolated aortitis is inflammation confined to the aortic wall without an identified systemic vasculitis or infection. Immune-mediated infiltration of the media and adventitia, frequently with giant cells and lymphoplasmacytic cells, damages elastic and smooth-muscle components of the wall. Loss of structural integrity weakens the aorta, predisposing to aneurysmal dilatation and dissection. Because it may represent a limited or early form of large-vessel vasculitis, some cases evolve into a recognised systemic disease over time.
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional aortic imaging with CT or MR angiography
Histology of resected aortic tissue with attention to giant cells and IgG4-positive plasma cells
Inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein)
Serum IgG4 to exclude an IgG4-related process
Screening for systemic large-vessel vasculitis including temporal artery assessment where indicated
PET imaging to assess extent of vascular inflammation
redFlags: Acute severe chest or back pain suggesting dissection or impending rupture
Rapid aneurysm enlargement on surveillance imaging
Systemic features heralding evolution to giant-cell or Takayasu arteritis
Aortic regurgitation from ascending aortic involvement
reference.prognosis: With surgical repair of the affected segment and appropriate immunosuppression when active inflammation persists, outcomes are generally favourable, but ongoing surveillance is essential because new aneurysms and dissection can develop elsewhere in the aorta.
pitfalls: Assuming resection is curative and abandoning imaging surveillance
Failing to check IgG4 and exclude an IgG4-related aortitis
Missing an underlying systemic large-vessel vasculitis
Overlooking infective aortitis before attributing inflammation to an idiopathic cause
references: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference vasculitis nomenclature
management: Surgical repair of the affected aortic segment when aneurysmal or dissecting, as is often identified at aneurysm surgery
Glucocorticoid therapy when active inflammation persists, with steroid-sparing immunosuppression for relapsing or steroid-dependent disease
Serial cross-sectional aortic imaging with CT or MR angiography to detect new aneurysm formation or dissection elsewhere in the aorta
Monitor inflammatory markers, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, to track disease activity
Screen for and monitor evolution into a systemic large-vessel vasculitis such as giant-cell arteritis, and exclude an IgG4-related process
Cardiovascular risk-factor control and blood-pressure management to reduce aortic wall stress
Multidisciplinary follow-up with rheumatology and vascular or cardiothoracic surgery
